content.description: For twenty years the United States poured enormous force into Vietnam to hold back communism. It got bogged down, tore itself apart, and left without winning.

hero.hook: The world's leading power, stuck in a war it could not win.

blocks.text: At the height of the war, **543,000** American soldiers are in Vietnam. And yet the world's leading power does not win. Twenty years of war, millions of dead, and in the end its opponent comes out on top. How is that possible?

blocks.caption: Look at this photo from 1966. It shows how America fights.

stops.text: Look at this photo from 1966. It shows how America fights.
**The helicopter.** Soldiers call it the “Huey.” The United States sends nearly 12,000 helicopters to Vietnam.
**The infantry.** Packs on their backs, they run to board. Within minutes they will be dropped deep in the jungle.
**Behind them, more aircraft are waiting.** Troops arrive in waves, anywhere, at any time.
Speed, power, technology. On paper, nothing can stand up to this.

blocks.text: Since the 19th century, Vietnam has been a French colony. In **1954**, after eight years of fighting, France loses the [[First Indochina War]] and leaves.

blocks.caption: Ho Chi Minh, around 1946. A communist and a nationalist, he led the fight against France. Now he wants a united, independent Vietnam.

steps.text: **Geneva, 1954.** The great powers meet to decide the country's fate.
They cut it in two at the **17th parallel**. The split is meant to be temporary: elections are planned for 1956 to reunite the country.
**In the North**, Ho Chi Minh leads a communist government, backed by the USSR and China. Its capital: Hanoi.
**In the South**, an authoritarian, anti-communist government, backed by the United States. Its capital: Saigon.
Two Vietnams, two sides of the Cold War. Each wants to reunite the country on its own terms.

blocks.text: Geneva, 1954. The great powers meet to decide the country's fate. They cut it in two at the 17th parallel. The split is meant to be temporary: elections are planned for 1956 to reunite the country. In the North, Ho Chi Minh leads a communist government, backed by the USSR and China. Its capital: Hanoi. In the South, an authoritarian, anti-communist government, backed by the United States. Its capital: Saigon. Two Vietnams, two sides of the Cold War. Each wants to reunite the country on its own terms.
The elections never happen: the South and Washington know Ho Chi Minh would win them. In the late 1950s, communist fighters take up arms in the South. Their enemies call them the [[Viet Cong]].
Washington is worried. In 1954, President Eisenhower sums up his fear with a simple picture: the [[domino theory]]. If Vietnam falls, its neighbors will fall one after another.

blocks.explanation: That is the domino theory. Washington does not want a colony: it wants an allied South Vietnam, so the rest of Asia does not tip over.
options: To take over the former French colony for itself.
Out of fear that communism will spread, one by one, to neighboring countries.
To get its hands on the region's oil.
blocks.prompt: So **why** does the United States get involved in Vietnam?
blocks.text: So **why** does the United States get involved in Vietnam? That is the domino theory. Washington does not want a colony: it wants an allied South Vietnam, so the rest of Asia does not tip over.

At first, America only sends military advisers: about **16,000** under President Kennedy. Then, on **August 2, 1964**, an American ship, the *Maddox*, is sailing off the northern coast, in the Gulf of Tonkin.

blocks.caption: This photo is taken that day from the deck of the Maddox. At first glance, an empty sea.

stops.text: This photo is taken that day from the deck of the *Maddox*. At first glance, an empty sea.
**On the horizon, two dark dots.** They are North Vietnamese torpedo boats, racing toward the ship.
**A third one, further left.** They fire their torpedoes, miss, and pull back under American fire.
That day, the attack is real. Two days later, things get murky.

blocks.text: On **August 4**, President Johnson is told of a second attack. It is night, the sea is rough, and the ships' messages contradict each other. Johnson does not wait: he orders air strikes on the North.
Three days later, Congress gives him, almost unanimously, the right to use force. We now know the second attack **never happened**.

blocks.caption: August 10, 1964. Johnson signs the text passed by Congress. He can now wage war without ever declaring it.

blocks.text: Johnson himself had doubts. A few days later he reportedly said in private: “For all I know, our Navy was shooting at whales out there.”
In **March 1965**, everything speeds up. American planes bomb the North almost without pause: this is Operation [[Rolling Thunder]]. The first combat troops land on the beach at Da Nang.

blocks.caption: Da Nang, August 1965. A young Marine waits on the beach during a landing.
Washington, April 1965. A press conference about the war.

stops.text: Washington, April 1965. A press conference about the war.
**Robert McNamara**, the U.S. Secretary of Defense. A former head of Ford, he believes in numbers, maps and charts.
**On the board**, a title: “North Vietnam bridge interdiction.” Each circle is an aerial photo of a targeted bridge.
**On the map**, his pointer follows Vietnam. His idea: cut from the air the roads that supply the South, until the North gives in.

blocks.explanation: From March 1965 to November 1968. The North repairs its bridges, scatters its depots, and does not give in.
blocks.prompt: The bombing of the North was planned for **eight weeks**. It lasted more than **three years**.
blocks.text: The bombing of the North was planned for **eight weeks**. It lasted more than **three years**. From March 1965 to November 1968. The North repairs its bridges, scatters its depots, and does not give in.

In three years, America goes from **23,000** to more than **500,000** soldiers on the ground. Its method has a name: “search and destroy.” Helicopters drop the troops, they hunt the enemy, then they leave.

On the other side, General **Giap**, head of the northern army, refuses the big battle. His men strike, then vanish into the jungle, the villages or tunnels. Ground won in the morning is lost again by night.

steps.text: To hold on, fighters in the South need weapons and men from the North. But the border at the 17th parallel is watched.
So the North goes around it. Thousands of kilometers of tracks cross Laos and Cambodia, two neighboring countries: this is the **Ho Chi Minh Trail**.
American planes bomb it relentlessly. Every night it is repaired. The supplies never stop.

blocks.text: To hold on, fighters in the South need weapons and men from the North. But the border at the 17th parallel is watched. So the North goes around it. Thousands of kilometers of tracks cross Laos and Cambodia, two neighboring countries: this is the Ho Chi Minh Trail. American planes bomb it relentlessly. Every night it is repaired. The supplies never stop.

blocks.caption: Since the enemy hides under the trees, the U.S. military decides to go after the trees.

stops.text: Since the enemy hides under the trees, the U.S. military decides to go after the trees.
**Three planes**, in formation, flying very low.
**Behind them, a cloud of weedkiller.** The best known is called Agent Orange. Nearly 80 million liters are sprayed in ten years.
**Below, fields and trees.** The goal: strip the leaves and destroy the crops. About 20% of the South's forests are hit, and the health effects are still felt today.

blocks.explanation: It wins almost every major engagement. It is the war it cannot win: the enemy replaces its losses and comes back.
blocks.prompt: The U.S. military **lost** most of the major battles of this war.
blocks.text: It wins almost every major engagement. It is the war it cannot win: the enemy replaces its losses and comes back.
Washington measures progress by counting enemy dead. But the North accepts far heavier losses than the United States does. Ho Chi Minh had warned the French twenty years earlier.
You will kill ten of us, we will kill one of you, and it is you who will tire of it first.
In late 1967, the U.S. government insists: victory is near. At home, though, doubt is growing.

blocks.caption: Washington, October 21, 1967. A crowd gathers against the war.

stops.text: Washington, October 21, 1967. A crowd gathers against the war.
**The sign says it all.** Many of the protesters are students, who can be drafted at any time.
**Across the pool, the crowd goes on.** About 100,000 people are there that day.

blocks.text: Three months later, on the night of **January 30, 1968**, the North and the Viet Cong strike where no one expects them.

steps.text: It is [[Tet]], the Vietnamese New Year. A truce has been announced. Many southern soldiers are on leave.
Within hours, more than **100 towns** and bases across the South are attacked at the same time.
**In Saigon**, a commando breaks into the grounds of the U.S. embassy. It is stopped within hours, but the images go around the world.
**In Hue**, the old imperial capital, the fighting lasts nearly a month.

blocks.text: It is Tet, the Vietnamese New Year. A truce has been announced. Many southern soldiers are on leave. Within hours, more than 100 towns and bases across the South are attacked at the same time. In Saigon, a commando breaks into the grounds of the U.S. embassy. It is stopped within hours, but the images go around the world. In Hue, the old imperial capital, the fighting lasts nearly a month.

blocks.caption: Saigon, 1968. South Vietnamese soldiers defend their capital during the offensive.

blocks.text: On the ground, the offensive fails: the towns are retaken and communist losses are huge. But every evening, Americans watch the fighting on television. They had been promised victory. The country's most trusted news anchor, Walter Cronkite, says it on air.
It seems now more certain than ever that the bloody experience of Vietnam is to end in a stalemate.

blocks.explanation: Tet is a military defeat for the North, but a victory in American public opinion. A month later, Johnson announces he will not run again.
options: Because the U.S. military runs short of soldiers.
Because Americans stop believing in the victory they were promised.
blocks.prompt: The North **loses** the battle of Tet. Why is it still a turning point?
blocks.text: The North **loses** the battle of Tet. Why is it still a turning point? Tet is a military defeat for the North, but a victory in American public opinion. A month later, Johnson announces he will not run again.

Elected in late 1968, President Nixon changes the plan: bring American soldiers home step by step and let the southern army fight alone. This is [[Vietnamization]]. The war still lasts four more years, and spills into Cambodia and Laos.

blocks.caption: Paris, January 27, 1973. After more than four years of talks, the United States signs its way out of Vietnam.

blocks.text: Without its protector, the South holds on for two years. In the spring of **1975**, the northern army launches its final assault. On **April 30**, its tanks roll into Saigon.

blocks.caption: April 29, 1975. Saigon is about to fall. In less than two days, the Americans evacuate more than 7,000 people by helicopter.

stops.text: April 29, 1975. Saigon is about to fall. In less than two days, the Americans evacuate more than 7,000 people by helicopter.
**Behind them, the helicopter** that has just dropped them on an American ship, out at sea.
**One bag in hand.** It is all they could take. In the years that follow, hundreds of thousands more will flee the country by sea.

blocks.text: Vietnam is reunited under a communist government, and Saigon becomes Ho Chi Minh City. The toll is terrible: between one and three million Vietnamese killed, civilians and soldiers.

blocks.caption: Washington, today. This black granite wall is the memorial to the American soldiers of Vietnam.

stops.text: Washington, today. This black granite wall is the memorial to the American soldiers of Vietnam.
**Names carved in the stone.** More than 58,000: every American killed or missing in the war.
**At the end of the path, the Washington Monument.** The wall points toward it: the defeat is written into the heart of the capital.

blocks.text: In the United States, people will long speak of the “Vietnam syndrome”: the fear of getting bogged down again in a distant war that force alone cannot win.

blocks.explanation: Twenty-one years separate the division of the country from its reunification.
items: Vietnam is split in two at Geneva

blocks.text: Twenty-one years separate the division of the country from its reunification.

The United States had the firepower. Its opponent refused open battle and never ran out of reinforcements.
Tet, lost on the ground by the North, turned American public opinion.
Twenty years of war, a country reunited under communism, and an America lastingly wary of distant wars.

Domino theory.explanation: American foreign politics theory according to which if one country became communist, its neighbors would fall one after another. It justified the commitment in Vietnam to "stop communist progression in Southeast Asia."

First Indochina War.explanation: From 1946 to 1954, France fought to keep its colony of Indochina, made up of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. It lost after its defeat at Dien Bien Phu.

Ho Chi Minh.explanation: Nationalist and communist leader, founder of the Viet-Minh (1941), first president of North Vietnam. His popular legitimacy as a liberator against the Japanese then the French gave him a politics advantage that the United States could never match.

Indochina War.explanation: Conflict (1946-1954) pitting France against the communist Viet Minh, resulting in French defeat and the independence of its former colonies.

January 1968.explanation: Simultaneous attack by the Viet Cong on more than 100 American cities during the Vietnamese New Year. Militarily a failure for Hanoi, it destroyed the credibility of the Johnson administration in the United States.

My Lai.explanation: Massacre of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by American soldiers in 1968, the revelation of which shocked world opinion.

Pentagon.explanation: Headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, by extension the American military command.

Rolling Thunder.explanation: The American bombing campaign against North Vietnam, from March 1965 to November 1968.

Tet.explanation: The Vietnamese New Year, the biggest holiday of the year. Both sides usually observed a truce for it.

Tet Offensive.explanation: Simultaneous Viet Cong attack on more than 100 American-held cities during the Vietnamese New Year. Militarily a failure for Hanoi, it destroyed the credibility of the Johnson administration in the United States.
